meta.title: tmux in a browser — your questions, answered
meta.description: Answers on attaching to tmux, mobile keyboard input, running coding agents, pairing and encryption, self-hosting, and what the free plan actually includes.

hero.title: Everything people ask before installing.
hero.lead: If your question isn't here, <mailLink>email us</mailLink> — we answer, and the good ones end up on this page.

items.question: Does mtmux replace tmux?
items.answer: No. It attaches to the tmux server you already run, the same way <cmd>tmux attach</cmd> does — with the <post>same sharp edges around resizing</post>. Remove mtmux and every session keeps running, untouched.

items.question: Do I need to install an app?
items.answer: No — the client is a web app. Add it to your home screen if you want fullscreen keyboard handling, but a normal browser tab works. Any current browser with WebSocket support is fine.

items.question: Do I need an account?
items.answer: No. Without one you get the CLI, local mode and the encrypted tunnel. <cmd>mtmux login</cmd> is optional and buys a dashboard and more than one registered server.

items.question: What does it need to run?
items.answer: Node 22 or newer and tmux. macOS, Linux with glibc or musl, and WSL2 are all supported — <post>installing tmux</post> covers every package manager. <cmd>mtmux doctor</cmd> checks the rest and tells you what is missing.

items.question: Does it work on a tablet?
items.answer: Yes, and it is arguably the best surface for it — real splits fit, and a Bluetooth keyboard passes chords through unmodified, prefix key included.

items.question: What about screen or zellij?
items.answer: tmux only. mtmux talks to the tmux server directly, so screen and zellij are not supported and there is no flag that enables them. If you are still deciding, the <post>tmux command reference</post> is the fastest way to judge whether tmux is the one you want.

items.question: Can I really type in vim on a phone?
items.answer: For edits, yes. The modifier row keeps esc, ctrl, alt, tab and the arrows reachable, and modifiers latch so chords are two taps. Writing a new module on a phone is still a bad idea — <post>what typing on a phone actually feels like</post> is the unvarnished version.

items.question: My layout is unreadable on a small screen.
items.answer: Turn on reflow: panes restack vertically and the focused one goes full width, without resizing the tmux window your desktop is attached to.

items.question: Does it survive the subway?
items.answer: The client reconnects and reattaches on its own when the network comes back, and the tmux session was never at risk — it kept running on your machine the whole time.

items.question: Do I have to enter the code every time?
items.answer: No. Pairing happens exactly once per browser: after that the browser holds a device key and reconnecting is a signed challenge. <cmd>mtmux devices</cmd> lists what is trusted, and revoke removes it.

items.question: Does mtmux notify me when Claude Code finishes?
items.answer: No. There is no push, no email, no Slack routing and no agent detection of any kind. mtmux gives you a session you can open from a phone in seconds and read — it is pull, not push, and we would rather say so than imply otherwise.

items.question: Then what does it do for agent runs?
items.answer: It removes the reason you had to be at your desk. The agent runs in a normal tmux session; you open the same pane from wherever you are, read what it printed, answer the prompt and start the next task.

items.question: Which agents does it support?
items.answer: All of them, because it does not know what an agent is. Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, aider or a shell script — if it runs in tmux, mtmux serves it, with no preset and no configuration.

items.question: Can I answer an approval prompt from my phone?
items.answer: Yes. It is an ordinary keystroke to an ordinary pane, so <cmd>y</cmd>, <cmd>n</cmd>, <cmd>ctrl-c</cmd> and your prefix key are all one tap on the modifier row.

items.question: I really do want to be paged. What should I use?
items.answer: Something built for it — a tmux hook that curls <cmd>ntfy</cmd>, or your agent's own hook support if it has any. <post>Paging yourself from tmux</post> is the full recipe. That composes with mtmux perfectly well: get paged by one thing, then open the session with the other.

items.question: Can the relay read my session?
items.answer: No. The session keys come out of a PAKE run between your machine and your browser, so the broker forwards sealed frames and holds no key. Details in the <link>threat model</link>.

items.question: Does the broker learn my pairing code?
items.answer: Only the first three digits. The code splits into a three-digit routing slot, which the broker assigns, and a six-digit secret generated in your browser that is never transmitted — not even as a hash. It is the password for the PAKE.

items.question: What stops someone guessing the secret?
items.answer: One wrong guess destroys the pairing. Both sides prove they derived the same key before anything else happens, and a failed confirmation ends it, so an attacker gets a single attempt at a million rather than an offline search. Guessing also costs the machine a visible warning and a slower replacement code, so a sweep is loud as well as futile.

items.question: Do I have to open a port?
items.answer: Nothing has to be forwarded or exposed to the internet. The CLI dials out, so there is no firewall hole, no VPN and no sshd facing the world. On a LAN it does listen locally so other devices in the house can reach it.

items.question: What if I lose my phone?
items.answer: <cmd>mtmux devices</cmd> lists the device ids this machine trusts and revoke forgets one, so that browser cannot reconnect. No password reset, and nothing left behind.

items.question: Can I run it fully self-hosted?
items.answer: Yes, at two levels. <cmd>mtmux start --local</cmd> serves your LAN and loopback and contacts no broker at all. If you want the tunnel too, run the broker yourself and point the CLI at it with <cmd>MTMUX_API_URL</cmd>. <post>Other ways to put tmux in a browser</post> covers the ttyd and wetty routes if you would rather not run ours.

items.question: Has the cryptography been audited?
items.answer: Not independently, and we will say so until it has been. The CPace implementation is checked against the draft's published test vectors, which proves the group maths — it does not prove the surrounding protocol. The source is MIT and readable.

items.question: Is it free?
items.answer: Free forever on one registered server with three trusted devices, and the encrypted tunnel is included rather than held back — 5 GB of relayed traffic a month. Anything on your own network is unmetered. <link>Pro</link> is $10/month or $100/year.

items.question: What happens if I hit the 5 GB?
items.answer: The relayed path stops until the month rolls over. Local and LAN access are unaffected, because that traffic never went through us in the first place.

items.question: Is it open source?
items.answer: The CLI and the browser client are MIT licensed. The pairing broker is in the same repository, so you can read it and run your own.

items.question: Who handles payments?
items.answer: Dodo Payments. Card details never reach our servers, and what Dodo shows at checkout is the authoritative price.
